title: The first battle

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vibhishana crosses, the brother who told the truth twice and then walked over. Walk across.

Some nights the noise doesn't stop. The neighbors are fighting, the baby won't sleep, your phone keeps lighting up, your own head won't quiet down. Lanka, now, is that loud. A golden city on a mountain, ringed with walls and moats, four great gates, each guarded by an army. Outside, on the plain, a sea of monkeys and bears, and two princes with bows. The talking is over. Angada's embassy failed. Vibhishana has told Rama where every gate is. At dawn, the monkeys rush the walls, climbing, hurling rocks and trees. And the fighting doesn't stop when the sun goes down.
screen: `THE GOLDEN CITY, WALLED.` → `FOUR GATES, FOUR ARMIES.` → `THE MONKEYS RUSH THE WALLS.`

segments.voice: Valmiki's war books are long, loud and crowded. Duel after duel: monkey against demon, champion against champion, names you'll never need to remember. The first day's fighting runs into the night, and that's when it gets frightening. The demons of Lanka are said to grow stronger in the dark. Nobody can see who's friend and who's enemy. Valmiki describes a terrible darkness filled with shouting, the clash of weapons, cries in the dark, rivers of blood. The monkeys lash out at shadows; some fight their own side by mistake. And in the middle of the chaos, the story keeps putting one image in front of us: Rama, steady. Arrows come from every side, and he answers them calmly, one at a time, as if the noise isn't touching him. Under the story runs a second one. A battle isn't only outside. The noise gets in, the fear gets in, the confusion gets in, and you start swinging at shadows. The Gita, which comes later on this path, has a word for the person who stays level in pleasure and pain, in noise and quiet: sthitaprajna, the one whose wisdom stands still. Rama, in this scene, is a picture of that. Not someone who's escaped the fight. Someone in the middle of it, still inside. The walls of Lanka won't fall for a long time; this is the first night of many. And already the question is not only who wins, but who can stay steady until morning.
screen: `THE FIGHTING RUNS INTO THE NIGHT.` · `IN THE DARK, SWINGING AT SHADOWS.` · `RAMA, STEADY, ONE ARROW AT A TIME.` · `STHITAPRAJNA: WISDOM THAT STANDS STILL.`

segments.voice: Don't try to make it quiet: let whatever noise is around you, traffic, voices, a hum, a fan, be there, and find your breath underneath it. Each time a sound grabs you, or your own mind is the noisy one, notice it and come back to one breath. You're not winning against the noise; you're staying level in it.
Sthitaprajna, the one whose wisdom stands still in pleasure and pain. Lanka's first battle runs into the dark, and one warrior stays steady inside it.
Your line: still, inside. The first night in Lanka is long, and morning is far off. Steady, till tomorrow.

howItsDone: The war in Lanka is staged over several nights in the Ramlila plays of north India that lead up to Dussehra; some readers take the battle both as a story and as a picture of the inner struggle to stay steady.

chat.says: What does it mean that Rama stayed steady in that night battle?
options: He stayed level inside, right in the middle of the chaos, not by escaping it.
He stayed out of the fighting until all the noise had died down.
He waited for morning light, when he could finally see whom to fight.
chat.meaning: Sthitaprajna is the one whose wisdom stands still. Rama hasn't escaped the fight; he's in the middle of it, still inside.

sthitaprajna.meaning: the one whose wisdom stands still, in pleasure and pain

Gita.meaning: the Bhagavad Gita, a sacred Hindu text that comes later on this path

Lanka.meaning: the island kingdom of Ravana, across the ocean

Vibhishana.meaning: Ravana's brother, who told Rama where every gate is

Valmiki.meaning: the sage traditionally credited with the oldest Ramayana

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (the siege of Lanka; the night battle, roughly sargas 41–44)

notes: The night battle and the rakshasas growing stronger at night follow Valmiki as remembered; confirm the sarga and the detail of monkeys striking their own side in the dark.
Linking Rama's steadiness to the Gita's sthitaprajna is the script's own framing (with 'many teachers read'); confirm it's acceptable.
The location of Valmiki's Lanka is left unstated; many identify it with Sri Lanka, and some scholars have proposed other places.
